Thorough to the root, this man. Even his tongue is a first-class weapon!

Sorimachi's analysis was exact. If we started an armored air battle here, the danger of getting precisely the result he described was high.

He had read it all the way through, and still he did not armor up and run. The reason had to be that he was allowing for the possibility that I would make the foolish choice as well: that I would insist on picking them off one by one, cut him down, and then hurry back as if there would be time.

Two days ago we had looked at each other for only an instant, but his armor was probably a military mass-production model. Presumably he had no guarantee of beating us for <ruby>speed<rt>legs</rt></ruby>.

In fact, I was confident I could catch him and cut him out of the sky. But I could not take the risk of leaving the mountain undefended. Armored combat was as good as shut to us.

With his tongue alone he had locked away our decisive strength, <ruby>and<rt>and</rt></ruby> he did not get proud over it either; he went on choosing careful moves. Whatever else he was, he had apparently been through more of these than I had.

I stopped Muramasa, stepped down onto the mountain road, and looked below.

A stream ran between the slopes, and half in it lay the man. His <ruby>armor<rt>bike</rt></ruby> was nowhere to be seen; from the marks around, the bike had rolled on farther down.

Sorimachi had no severe external injuries. The water must have softened the impact, because for a fall from that height the result was almost a miracle. Muramasa's exasperation was understandable.

He did not move; perhaps he was unconscious. But looking closely, only the fingertips of his right hand were crawling, as if looking for something. They scratched the dirt of the bank in vain.

A little way off, the blade of his sword cane stood in a tree trunk.
